title: Shipping copy on a product page
excerpt: Put the delivery window and the cost on the product page, beside the price. A shipping surprise later in checkout is how carts get abandoned after the product has done its job.
alt: Three pale speckled bottles on a gray surface, two holding dried seed heads. The objects are specific, which is the standard a shipping line should meet.
caption: Specific objects, the way a delivery line should be specific. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Where should shipping information appear?
faqs.answer: Put the usual delivery window and the cost, or the rule that sets the cost, on the product page near the price. Checkout may confirm the exact figure for an address. It should not be the first time the shopper sees that a cost or a wait exists.

faqs.question: What counts as a delivery window?
faqs.answer: A window names days a person can picture, and says whether they are business days. Leaving in two business days and arriving in four to six is a window. The phrase standard shipping is not, because it does not say when the object will show up.

faqs.question: What if the cost depends on the address?
faqs.answer: Say the rule and give a starting figure for the region you sell most, then show the exact shipping and tax in the bag before the card field. People can accept an estimate. They leave when the first real number appears beside payment.

markdown:
Shipping information ecommerce belongs on the product page, in the same glance as the price. Put the delivery window and the cost where the person decides, before they start a checkout. A surprise in the bag is how a cart gets abandoned after the product has already done its job.

The shopper is not asking for a carrier contract. They are asking two questions. When does this arrive, and what do I pay to have it sent. If those answers exist only after an address form, the product page is unfinished.

## Where the decision actually happens

The product page is where someone commits to the object. Shipping is part of that commitment, the same way size and materials are. “Calculated at checkout” can be true and still be the wrong sentence, because it withholds the fact the decision needs.

[Baymard Institute’s compilation](https://baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate) of fifty studies, last updated in September 2025, puts the average documented cart abandonment rate at 70.22 percent. The same page separates causes. In Baymard’s quantitative study, 42 percent of US online shoppers had abandoned a cart because they were browsing or not ready to buy. That share is mostly unavoidable. Extra costs such as shipping, tax, and fees sit at 40 percent. Delivery that felt too slow sits at 20 percent. Being unable to see the total up front sits at 12 percent. Those three are the reasons a shipping sentence on the product page can change.

Place the lines under the price, or in a short block the thumb can reach without hunting the footer. One line for the window. One line for the cost, or for the rule that determines the cost. Link the full policy for the person who wants the edge cases. Do not make the link the only place the numbers exist.

A founder often learns the real window from the warehouse, then writes it once in a FAQ nobody opens from the product. Move the sentence. The FAQ can keep the exceptions. The product page keeps the usual case.

## A window a person can picture

“Standard shipping” is not a window. Name what you know in days, and say whether those days are business days. “Leaves in two business days. Arrives in four to six.” If you only control the moment it leaves your hands, say that, and do not invent the carrier’s half of the trip.

Made-to-order and preorder need their own window, on the products that are made to order or preorder. A shop-wide “ships in 48 hours” that is false for the object on screen will be felt at the worst moment, in the tracking email. If the object ships from a different place than the rest of the line, say so when that changes the date.

Cutoff times belong in the same block when they change the promise. “Order by 2 p.m. Eastern to leave today” is useful. A countdown that resets in a way you do not honor is not. If you cannot keep the cutoff on busy days, describe the ordinary case and leave the clock off.

International shoppers need to see whether you ship to them before they fall in love with the object. A country note near the shipping lines is enough. “We ship to the US and Canada. Other countries, see the policy.” If you do not ship to them, say that on the product page, not after they have typed a card.

Returns and duties can be one clause each if they change the decision. The long version still lives on its own page. The product page earns the right to be short by being specific.

## Cost, thresholds, and the number they will remember

Say the cost in the brand’s currency, next to the window. If shipping is free, say free, and say over what if there is a threshold. “Free shipping over $80” on the product page lets someone do the math while they are still choosing a second item. The same sentence hidden in a banner they closed is not on the page.

If the price depends on region, say the rule and show an example for the region you sell most. “Ground shipping in the US starts at $8.” You can refine it in the bag once you know the postal code. You should not open with silence. Baymard’s “could not see the total up front” reason is often this gap. People will tolerate an estimate. They leave when the first real number appears beside the card field.

Tax is a sibling fact. If tax is added later, say that it is added at checkout for their state, so the shipping line is not blamed for a jump it did not cause. If your prices include tax, say that too. The point is that the number on the product page and the number on the card screen should feel like the same price plus a rule you already disclosed.

Free-shipping thresholds should use the same figure everywhere: product page, bag, and announcement. Three different thresholds read as a trick even when the cause is an old banner. Pick the rule your warehouse and your payment settings actually implement.

Heavy, oversized, or freight items need their own cost line. A flat rate that is a lie for one product will be the review people remember. If you must quote those after a conversation, the product page should say “Shipping is quoted before you pay,” and the path should be a person, not a checkout that invents a number.

## What the bag is allowed to do

Checkout may confirm the window and the cost. It should not introduce them. By the time someone reaches the bag, they should recognize the figures. The bag’s job is to apply the rule to this address: the exact service, the exact price, the exact tax.

Show the shipping method with a date range, not only a carrier brand. People know their own deadline better than they know a logo. If you offer a faster method, show its price beside the slower one so the choice is a comparison, not a discovery.

Do not add a handling fee under a new name at this step. If a fee exists, it belonged beside the price. Baymard groups shipping, tax, and fees together as extra costs. A fee with a cute label is still an extra cost, and it is the category most often named when people explain why they left.

Guest checkout should not be the moment shipping copy gets longer. The account wall is a separate problem. Keep the shipping summary visible above the fold of the bag on a phone. A summary stuck under a promo-code field will not be seen by the person who is already anxious about the total.

If a method is unavailable for the address, say why, and offer the method that is available. “We can’t ship overnight to that postal code. Ground arrives in four to six business days, at $8.” That is a correction. A silent removal of the fast option feels like the price changed.

## The products that need a different sentence

Preorder: say the ship window as a range you can keep, and say that the charge happens now or when it ships, whichever is true. Do not reuse the in-stock sentence.

Split shipments: if a bag can leave in two boxes, say whether that changes the cost. A second box that adds a second fee should be disclosed before payment, ideally as soon as the second item is in the bag.

Local pickup: if you offer it, it is a shipping method with a cost of zero and a window of its own. “Ready at the studio in two business days” is a window. “Pickup available” is not.

Digital goods beside physical goods: say that the file arrives by email and the object ships. One blended “delivery” line will be wrong for half the order.

Down the Cove, the public ecommerce migration and redesign in Hanabi’s work, is a reminder that shipping copy is part of the shop system, not a footer inherited from the old platform. Whatever you replatform, rewrite the sentence for the way you actually send goods now.

Someone on the team has to own updates. Holiday cutoffs, a new warehouse, a carrier change. The product-page lines should be editable without a developer if they change often, and they should be checked when they do. A beautiful component full of last year’s promise is a defect.

## A check on one real product

Open the product you sell most, on a phone, as a person who has never heard of you.

1. Find the delivery window without opening the footer.
2. Find the cost, or the rule that sets the cost, in the same area.
3. Add it to the bag and see whether the figures match what you just read.
4. Change the address to another region you claim to serve and read the new total before you touch a card field.
5. Read the line aloud. If you would not say it at a counter, rewrite it.

The page is ready when a skeptical person can repeat the promise without opening a policy. The policy still exists for the exceptions. It is not a substitute for the two lines.

The other promise shoppers look for beside shipping is how a return works if the object is wrong. [A returns policy written like a person](/blog/a-returns-policy-written-like-a-person) is the next piece, because a clear delivery line still loses the sale when the return terms are a document nobody can read.
